title: Sednit_Xagent_Incident_Response_6ab
description: Investigate a compromised network where the Sednit group's Xagent malware has been detected. Identify the malware, understand its behavior, and contain the threat.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of Linux system administration
Basic knowledge of systemd service management
outcomes: Discovering command and control communication ports

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
The Sednit group, also known as APT29, is a sophisticated cyber espionage group believed to be operating out of Russia. They are known for targeting government agencies, diplomatic organizations, and research institutions. The Sednit group uses a variety of malware, including Xagent, a backdoor malware capable of establishing persistent connections to command and control (C2) servers, executing commands, and exfiltrating data.

In this scenario, you will investigate a compromised network where the Sednit group's Xagent malware has been detected. Your goal is to identify the malware, understand its behavior, and contain the threat.

This scenario follows a progressive difficulty structure, starting with basic service discovery and advancing to more complex persistence and C2 communication analysis. The attack chain covered includes initial access, persistence mechanisms, and command and control communication. The techniques used are accurate representations of real-world malware behavior.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: Users have reported slow performance on the `target` host. Investigate and identify any unauthorized or suspicious services running on this host. The flag is the name of the suspicious service.

hints.title: Conceptual hint
hints.content: Suspicious services often have unusual or unfamiliar names. Look for services that don't match the typical system services.

hints.title: Directional hint
hints.content: Systemd services can be listed using the systemctl command. Focus on the service names rather than their status.

hints.title: Near-spoiler hint
hints.content: Try the command: systemctl list-units --type=service | grep -v 'systemd|dbus|sshd'

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: Now that you have identified the suspicious service, determine how it is automatically started after reboot. The flag is the path to the service configuration file.

hints.title: Conceptual hint
hints.content: Persistence mechanisms often involve service configuration files that define how and when a service should start.

hints.title: Directional hint
hints.content: Systemd service status can reveal the configuration file location. Look for the 'Loaded' line in the status output.

hints.title: Near-spoiler hint
hints.content: Try the command: systemctl status bkd.service | grep 'Loaded'

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (Port)
levels.content: The suspicious service appears to be communicating with an external command and control server. Determine which network port is used for this communication. The flag is the port number.

hints.title: Conceptual hint
hints.content: Command and control communication typically involves network ports that are listening for incoming connections.

hints.title: Directional hint
hints.content: Network ports can be listed using the ss command. Focus on the listening ports (LISTEN state).

hints.title: Near-spoiler hint
hints.content: Try the command: ss -tulnp | grep LISTEN
